tasks.name: Use pointer relationships to eliminate or compact candidates

concepts.name: Opposing two pointers
concepts.description: Use ordered structure to move left/right boundaries and discard groups of impossible candidates without checking every pair.

concepts.name: Read/write pointers
concepts.description: Scan input with one pointer while another marks where the next accepted or compacted item should be written.

concepts.name: Fast/slow pointer relationship
concepts.description: Maintain two traversals with different rates or a fixed gap to detect cycles, midpoints, or relative-position properties.

concepts.name: Fixed sliding window
concepts.description: Maintain state for one contiguous region of constant size by adding the entering item and removing the leaving item.

concepts.name: Variable sliding window
concepts.description: Expand one boundary and move the other only as needed to restore a validity condition that supports monotonic repair.

concepts.name: Window pattern discrimination
concepts.description: Distinguish moving-window problems from prefix-state queries and other range methods based on contiguity, overlap, and whether validity can be repaired by boundary movement.

concepts.name: Sort and merge intervals
concepts.description: Sort ranges by a boundary so overlap with the current merged frontier can be decided in one scan.

concepts.name: Interval endpoint semantics
concepts.description: Treat open, closed, and half-open endpoints according to the contract because endpoint-touching may or may not count as overlap.

questions.prompt: A sorted array contains job sizes. You need any pair whose sizes sum exactly to a capacity. The solution should use O(1) extra space. Which approach best fits?
questions.explanation: Because the values are sorted, comparing the smallest and largest candidates lets you safely discard one boundary after each comparison. This gives a linear scan with O(1) extra state.
hints: The sorted order should justify which side can be discarded.

error_codes.description: The selected method does not best use the sorted-order plus O(1)-space constraints.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 3: Sets and Sorting
MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

choice_feedback.two: Correct: order lets each comparison eliminate one boundary.
choice_feedback.hash: Hash lookup can be linear time, but it uses O(n) extra state and ignores the explicit space constraint.
choice_feedback.nested: All-pairs scanning is correct but O(n²).
choice_feedback.binary: Binary-searching for a complement for each item is O(n log n), slower than the two-pointer scan.

choices.label: Start at both ends and move one boundary based on whether the sum is too small or too large
Build a hash map of all job sizes first
Check every pair with nested loops
For each job size, binary-search the rest of the array for its complement

questions.prompt: For sorted values `[1, 3, 4, 7, 10]` and target `11`, order the opposing-pointer states until the pair is found.
questions.explanation: 1 + 10 equals 11 immediately, so the first boundary comparison finds the pair. The initial state comes before the sum evaluation and successful return.
hints: Evaluate the two endpoints before moving either pointer.

error_codes.description: The pointer trace is out of order.

items.label: Return the pair because the sum equals the target

questions.prompt: A mutable array of records contains tombstones. Compact all non-deleted records to the front IN PLACE while preserving their relative order. Which state best fits?
questions.explanation: One pointer reads every item, while a write pointer advances only when a kept record is copied. That preserves stable order and produces a compact prefix without a second array.
hints: One position needs to inspect input; another needs to mark the next accepted output slot.

error_codes.description: The selected state does not directly provide stable in-place compaction.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 2: Data Structures and Dynamic Arrays

choice_feedback.rw: Correct: read scans input; write marks the next compacted position.
choice_feedback.ends: Opposing pointers can reorder records and do not naturally preserve stable order here.
choice_feedback.set: A set does not represent output positions or stable order.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting changes relative order and does not express deletion filtering.

choices.label: Read pointer over every record + write pointer that advances only for kept records
Swap records from the left and right ends toward the center
Put all surviving record IDs in a set
Sort records by deletion flag and then take a prefix

questions.prompt: A stable in-place filter should copy only active records into the compacted prefix. Flag the update that breaks the write-pointer invariant.
questions.explanation: The write pointer must advance only after an accepted record occupies the next compacted slot. Advancing it for a discarded record leaves a hole in the output prefix.
hints: After each step, `records[:write]` should contain exactly the kept records processed so far.

error_codes.description: The update that creates holes in the compacted prefix was not identified.
A valid read/write step was incorrectly flagged.

questions.prompt: A configuration object forms a linked chain: each state has exactly one `next` reference or `None`. You must detect whether the chain contains a cycle using O(1) extra memory. Which approach fits?
questions.explanation: With one deterministic next link per state, a slow pointer and a fast pointer can detect a cycle using constant extra state: if a cycle exists and both enter it, their relative movement eventually makes them meet.
hints: The O(1)-memory requirement rules out remembering every visited object.

error_codes.description: The selected approach does not satisfy the single-next-chain plus O(1)-memory constraints as directly.

source_refs.title: Wikipedia — Cycle detection

choice_feedback.floyd: Correct: the single-next chain supports fast/slow cycle detection.
choice_feedback.set: A visited set works but needs O(n) extra memory.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting is not defined for following object references and does not detect a cycle.
choice_feedback.bfs: A general graph traversal is unnecessary for a single deterministic next-link chain and normally needs visited state.

choices.label: Move one pointer one step and another two steps; detect whether they meet
Store every visited object in a set
Sort the states by identifier
Run a breadth-first traversal with a visited set

questions.prompt: A mutable sorted array may contain duplicate IDs. Replace it IN PLACE with one copy of each ID, preserve sorted order, and return the new logical length. Which design best fits?
questions.explanation: Because equal IDs are adjacent, a read pointer can scan once while a write pointer advances only when a new distinct ID is accepted. This preserves stable sorted order with O(1) extra state.

error_codes.description: The selected approach does not best satisfy stable in-place deduplication.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 2: Data Structures and Dynamic Arrays
MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 3: Sets and Sorting

choice_feedback.rw: Correct: it uses sorted adjacency and compacts unique IDs in place.
choice_feedback.set: A set finds uniqueness but does not by itself satisfy stable in-place array compaction.
choice_feedback.resort: The input is already sorted; copying and resorting adds unnecessary work and space.
choice_feedback.ends: Swapping from opposite ends can destroy stable ordering.

choices.label: Read every ID; write only when the current ID differs from the last kept ID
Convert the array to a set and return the set size
Copy the array, remove duplicates, then sort the copy again

questions.prompt: You need the largest total across every contiguous block of exactly 5 telemetry readings. Which approach avoids recomputing almost-identical blocks?
questions.explanation: Each size-5 window differs from the previous one by exactly one outgoing and one incoming reading. Maintaining the rolling sum makes each move constant additional work.
hints: Neighboring candidates have the same size and overlap in four of five positions.

error_codes.description: The selected method does not most directly exploit the overlap between same-size neighboring windows.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 2: Data Structures and Dynamic Arrays
MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

choice_feedback.window: Correct: update only the entering and leaving readings.
choice_feedback.resum: This repeats four of the five additions for neighboring windows.
choice_feedback.prefix: Prefix sums can answer fixed ranges too, but for one sequential pass the rolling window stores less auxiliary state and directly exploits overlap.

choices.label: Maintain the current 5-reading sum; add the entering reading and subtract the leaving one
Sum all 5 readings from scratch for every starting index
Build a full prefix array even though only one sequential maximum scan is needed
Sort all readings and take the largest 5

questions.prompt: Request timestamps are sorted. For each new request, you need the count of requests in the trailing 60 seconds. Which boundary rule best maintains the active range?
questions.explanation: The right boundary advances with each new timestamp. While the oldest request is at least 60 seconds behind the current timestamp, move the left boundary forward to expire it.
hints: The oldest requests are the only ones that can become invalid as time advances.

error_codes.description: The selected boundary rule does not maintain the trailing valid request range.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 2: Data Structures and Dynamic Arrays

choice_feedback.expire: Correct: ordered timestamps make left-to-right expiration monotonic.
choice_feedback.sort: The timestamps are already ordered; resorting each time repeats unnecessary work.
choice_feedback.reset: Resetting loses still-valid requests that should remain in the active range.
choice_feedback.prefix: A static prefix total does not by itself identify which old timestamps have expired relative to the current request.

choices.label: Advance right with each request; while the oldest timestamp is outside the 60-second range, advance left

questions.prompt: Values may be positive or negative. You need to know whether ANY contiguous interval sums exactly to a target. Why is the rule “if the sum is too large, always move left forward” not generally valid?
questions.explanation: With signed values, removing the left item can increase or decrease the sum, so 'too large' does not imply that shrinking moves predictably toward the target. Prefix-state methods do not require that monotonic repair property.
hints: Ask what happens if the item removed from the left is negative.

error_codes.description: The selected reason does not identify the missing monotonic repair property.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

choice_feedback.signed: Correct: signed values break the simple monotonic shrink rule.
choice_feedback.contiguous: Contiguity alone is not enough to justify variable-window repair.
choice_feedback.hash: The issue is not whether a hash table is available; it is whether boundary movement predictably repairs validity.
choice_feedback.length: Window length can still be tracked; that is not the failure.

choices.label: Removing a negative left value could increase the sum, so shrinking is not predictably corrective
Because the candidate interval is contiguous
Because hash tables cannot store signed values
Because a window cannot track its length

questions.prompt: A file contains positive request sizes in arrival order. Find the longest contiguous run whose total size is at most 8 MiB. Which approach best preserves arrival contiguity and avoids restarting the sum for every start position?
questions.explanation: Because sizes are positive, expanding right can only increase the total and moving left can only decrease it. Maintain one contiguous active range and shrink only when it exceeds the budget.

error_codes.description: The selected approach does not best exploit positive-size monotonicity while preserving contiguity.

questions.prompt: Why does sorting intervals by start allow a one-pass merge against the current merged frontier?
questions.explanation: Once starts are nondecreasing, the next interval cannot begin before an unseen future interval. If it begins after the current merged end, the current merged interval is final; otherwise the new interval overlaps the current frontier and can extend its end.
hints: Think about what start-order proves about unseen intervals.
